phase1.explanation:
Every single class you write in Java, whether you realize it or not, already inherits three methods from `Object`: `toString()`, `equals()`, and `hashCode()`. Left un-overridden, [[warn:they're not very useful]] — default `toString()` just prints something like `Person@1a2b3c`, and default `equals()` only checks whether two references point to the exact same object in memory, same as `==`.

Overriding `toString()` is the easy one: [[key:whatever String you return is what gets printed automatically]] any time you do `System.out.println(someObject)` or concatenate it into a String.

`equals()` is where it gets more careful: you're defining what "equal" actually MEANS for your class — here, two Persons count as equal if their name and age both match, regardless of whether they're literally the same object in memory.

And here's the rule that catches people off guard: [[warn:if you override equals(), you must override hashCode() too, and keep them consistent]] — [[key:whenever two objects are equal() to each other, their hashCode() values must also be equal]]. Skip this, and hash-based collections like `HashSet` and `HashMap` will misbehave — look at the example: without a matching hashCode(), a HashSet can't tell that p1 and p2 are "the same" Person, and quietly stores a duplicate.

phase2.errorMessage:
false
Set size: 2

(No compiler error — but the LOGIC is wrong! Duplicates can appear in HashSet.)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Without overriding equals() and hashCode(), Person falls back to Object's defaults]] — which compare by memory reference, not content. `p1` and `p2` hold identical data, but they're two separate objects, so default `equals()` says false, and default `hashCode()` gives them two different values entirely.

That's exactly why the `HashSet` ends up with 2 entries instead of 1: [[key:HashSet uses hashCode() first to find the right "bucket," then equals() to check for an actual duplicate within it]] — and both checks fail here, so it just adds p2 as if it were a totally different Person. [[key:The fix is overriding both methods together, and keeping them logically consistent]] — never just one or the other.

mcq.question:
If you override equals() for a class, what's the rule about hashCode()?

A) You should leave hashCode() at its default
B) You must override hashCode() too, and equal objects must produce equal hash codes
C) hashCode() is unrelated to equals() and can be ignored
D) You should delete hashCode() entirely

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a Book class with:
• Fields: title (String), author (String)
• Constructor
• Override toString() — returns "Book[title='X', author='Y']"
• Override equals() — based on title AND author
• Override hashCode() — consistent with equals

In main, create two identical books and test equals() and toString().

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: that habit of multiplying by 31 when writing a hashCode() isn't arbitrary — 31 is an odd prime, which helps spread hash values out evenly and avoid collisions, and multiplying by it can be optimized by the JVM into a bit-shift plus a subtraction, which used to matter more for performance than it does today. It's still the convention you'll see in nearly every generated hashCode() method.
